prompt.context: Syzygy Supercomputers is a large international fully-integrated computers and communications company with annual revenues of approximately $20 billion U.S. In the past several years, the company has seen a steady decline in profits.
prompt.question: The CEO has asked us to look into this problem. How can Syzygy Supercomputers get back on track?

clarifying_info.q: What products or segments does Syzygy operate in?
clarifying_info.a: Only the information already provided is available; other information is currently unavailable.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape like?
clarifying_info.a: There are several players in the market, but everything has remained stable from a competitive standpoint.

clarifying_info.q: How do Syzygy's COGS and SG&A compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: COGS, SG&A, and other profitability factors are on-par with competitors, except for R&D — the candidate should ask specifically about R&D.

exhibits.title: Syzygy's Historical Costs, Revenues and Profits
exhibits.shows: A historical time-series chart showing Syzygy's revenues, costs, and profits over several years, illustrating the trend of declining profitability
exhibits.data: Revenue ~$20B; multi-year historical breakdown of costs and profits showing a steady profit decline

exhibits.title: Worldwide Telecom Computing Market (Today)
exhibits.shows: A market map displaying the size of each product segment in the worldwide telecom computing market and Syzygy's position (rectangle heights) relative to competitors across five product categories
exhibits.data: Five product categories shown; rectangle heights represent market share; competitors' rectangles shown alongside Syzygy's

exhibits.title: Syzygy's Absolute vs. Relative Market Share
exhibits.shows: A bubble chart plotting Syzygy's five product lines on two axes — Absolute Market Share (x-axis) and Relative Market Share (y-axis, Syzygy share divided by closest competitor's share) — with bubble size proportional to Syzygy's total revenues in that category
exhibits.data: Five bubbles corresponding to five products; x-axis = absolute market share; y-axis = relative market share (>1 means Syzygy is market leader); bubble diameter = Syzygy revenue in that segment

exhibits.title: Companies' R&D vs. Degree of Technical Leadership
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot comparing R&D spending levels to perceived degree of technical leadership for major industry competitors, with a normative band indicating expected relationship
exhibits.data: Multiple competitors plotted; a normative band shown; Syzygy's position relative to competitors and the normative band is visible

exhibits.title: Syzygy's R&D Expenses and Selling Prices for Supercomputers
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of Syzygy's R&D expenses by feature category alongside the selling prices (or customer willingness to pay) associated with those features for its supercomputer product line
exhibits.data: R&D expense amounts per feature; corresponding selling price or willingness-to-pay data per feature; reveals which features generate revenue vs. which do not

framework: 1. Examine historical financial performance: confirm revenue and profit trends over time to establish the nature and magnitude of the profitability decline
2. Assess market dynamics and competitive positioning: understand segment sizes, Syzygy's market share by product, and relative competitive standing
3. Deep-dive into cost and revenue drivers: evaluate COGS, SG&A, and — critically for a hi-tech company — R&D spending relative to competitors and returns generated
4. Identify the root cause: determine whether R&D is generating customer willingness to pay commensurate with the investment
5. Develop recommendations: advise on R&D reallocation or reduction, and on portfolio rationalization (exit weak segments, double down on market-leadership positions)

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 1. What does the historical financial data tell you about the nature of the profitability problem?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that revenues appear roughly stable at ~$20B while profits have declined steadily, pointing to a cost-side problem rather than a revenue collapse. Candidate should explicitly ask for historical trends (not just current profitability) and use the chart to confirm the cost structure has worsened over time.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibits 2 and 3 together, identify which product corresponds to which bubble. What does this tell you about Syzygy's portfolio?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 2 shows absolute market share (rectangle height) and relative market share (ratio of Syzygy's rectangle to competitors') per product. Exhibit 3 plots these same two dimensions as axes with bubble size = Syzygy revenue in that segment. Correct mapping: Product #1 = Custom Applications, Product #2 = Supercomputers, Product #3 = Telecom Equipment, Product #4 = Satellites, Product #5 = Operating Software. Candidate should note that Operating Software (Product #5) has low absolute and low relative market share — a weak competitive position subject to economies of scale, network economics, and the experience curve working against Syzygy.

questions.prompt: What is the key insight from Exhibit 4 about Syzygy's R&D spending?
questions.guidance: Syzygy is the only major competitor whose R&D spending falls below the normative band relating R&D investment to perceived technical leadership. Despite spending slightly more on R&D than Cray Research and Sonic Wave, Syzygy enjoys less customer perception of technical leadership than those peers. This signals that Syzygy is not getting the expected return on its R&D investment — the spending is misallocated, not necessarily insufficient in total.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 5, what is the specific problem with Syzygy's R&D spending in supercomputers?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 5 shows that Syzygy is spending R&D dollars on features that do not generate customer willingness to pay — the R&D expense on those features exceeds the incremental selling price (or price premium) they command. Correct analysis identifies that the absolute R&D expense (not just the percentage) on certain features is wasteful because customers are not willing to pay for them at a level that covers the development cost.

math.setup: Compare R&D expense per feature to the incremental customer willingness-to-pay (selling price uplift) per feature. Features where R&D cost > willingness-to-pay represent value-destroying investment.
steps: Identify features where R&D spend > incremental selling price from Exhibit 5
Sum the R&D expense on those features to quantify wasted spend
Compare total wasted R&D to the observed profit decline to confirm this explains the problem
math.answer: Features with R&D cost exceeding customer willingness-to-pay represent the primary source of profit leakage; eliminating or redirecting that spending would restore profitability.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options does Syzygy have to address its R&D problem and broader portfolio?

categories.name: R&D Reallocation
ideas: Cut R&D spending on features that customers are not willing to pay for
Redirect R&D budget toward features that generate measurable willingness-to-pay above cost
Implement a feature-level ROI hurdle rate before committing R&D resources
Use customer research and conjoint analysis to prioritize features by willingness-to-pay

categories.name: Portfolio Rationalization
ideas: Exit the Operating Software segment (Product #5) where Syzygy has low absolute and low relative market share
Focus investment on segments where Syzygy is the market leader (high relative market share) to leverage economies of scale and the experience curve
Selectively divest or partner in weak segments to free up capital for core strengths

categories.name: Competitive Positioning
ideas: Double down on Supercomputers and other leader segments to widen the competitive moat
Use cost savings from R&D cuts to fund targeted price competition or marketing in leadership segments
Explore adjacent applications where Syzygy's technical capabilities translate to high customer willingness-to-pay

recommendation: Syzygy should cut or redirect R&D spending away from features that customers are not willing to pay for, immediately reducing the main driver of margin deterioration
Syzygy should exit the Operating Software business (Product #5) given its weak market position and unfavorable economics from scale, network effects, and the experience curve
Syzygy should concentrate resources on the product categories where it holds market leadership to leverage economies of scale and reinforce its competitive advantage
risks: Cutting R&D may slow future innovation if the feature prioritization framework is not carefully designed
Exiting Operating Software may disrupt bundled customers or existing contracts that depend on the software
Competitors may increase R&D in vacated areas, eroding Syzygy's technical leadership perception
next_steps: Conduct detailed feature-level willingness-to-pay analysis across all product lines, not just supercomputers
Develop a transition plan for the Operating Software divestiture, including customer communication and contract wind-down
Establish an R&D portfolio governance process with regular ROI reviews tied to customer pricing data
